name: Yayoi culture
title: The story of the Yayoi culture

text: About 2,300 years ago, farmers in northern Kyushu, the part of Japan closest to Korea, began growing rice in wet fields.
Many farmers had come from Korea and other lands, and they mixed with the Jōmon people already living there.
src: c. 300 BCE: The conventional start of the Yayoi period, as wet-rice farming spreads from northern Kyushu / The earliest sites, Itazuke and Nabata, lie in northern Kyushu, the part of Japan closest to Korea
Farming migrants from the Korean Peninsula and other parts of the continent mixed with the Jōmon population

text: Growing rice let people stay in one place, in villages that lasted.
Some lived in houses with thatched roofs, raised up off the ground.
src: led people to stay in one place for long periods in permanent farming villages
lived in raised-floor dwellings with thatched roofs

text: Craftsmen learned to work bronze and iron, and cast bronze bells, mirrors and swords.
Their pots were plainer and more practical than those of the Jōmon.
src: Techniques for bronze and iron were introduced, and Yayoi craft specialists made bronze ceremonial bells (dōtaku), mirrors and weapons / the bronze sword
Yayoi pottery is simpler and more practical than the richly decorated wares of the Jōmon

text: Rice farming spread from Kyushu to Honshu and other parts of Japan.
Some families grew rich from land and stored grain, and fighting led many villages to build moats.
src: beginning in northern Kyushu and spreading to Honshu

Owning land and storing grain allowed people to accumulate wealth / They also called the society one of violent struggles, and archaeology points the same way: many excavated settlements were moated or built on hilltops

text: Chinese books tell of their land, called Wa, and of Queen Himiko, a spiritual leader who ruled it.
A golden seal that a Chinese emperor sent to one Yayoi state was later found in Kyushu.
src: Chinese histories describe the land of Wa / Queen Himiko took the throne of Wa as a spiritual leader
The golden seal that Emperor Guangwu of the Later Han dynasty gave to the Na state of Wo in 57 CE, recorded in the Book of the Later Han, was found in northern Kyushu in the 18th century.

text: About 1,700 years ago the Yayoi age ended, when keyhole-shaped burial mounds began to be built.
Together with the Jōmon, the newcomers became the ancestors of the Japanese people of today.
src: mid-3rd century CE: The first keyhole-shaped burial mounds mark the transition to the Kofun period
The migrants of the Yayoi period gradually merged with the native Jōmon population, forming the foundation of the modern Japanese people.
